title: What are the KISS ("Keep It Simple, Stupid") and YAGNI ("You Aren't Gonna Need It") principles: KISS says prefer the simplest solution that works (avoid unnecessary abstraction, over-engineering, or clever code), YAGNI says don't build features or abstractions until they are actually needed (premature generalization wastes effort and adds complexity): and how do you balance them against DRY (DRY can lead to premature abstraction if you extract a shared module for two things that only look similar today), and what are real examples of YAGNI violations (building a plugin architecture for a service that will only ever have one implementation, adding a message broker when direct REST calls suffice)?
shortTitle: KISS and YAGNI principles, balancing them against DRY, and real YAGNI violations
keyPoints: KISS: the simplest solution that correctly solves the problem is usually the best, because simple code is easier to read, test, and change.
YAGNI: do not build features or abstractions on speculation about future needs; build only what today's requirement demands.
DRY applied too eagerly conflicts with KISS and YAGNI by tempting premature abstraction.
Rule of three: wait until the same knowledge genuinely repeats three times before unifying.
YAGNI violations: plugin architecture for one implementation, Kafka when REST suffices, caching before measuring.
Default stance: KISS and YAGNI first, apply DRY only when knowledge genuinely repeats and changes together.

s1_definition.oneliner: KISS says prefer the simplest thing that works, YAGNI says do not build it until you actually need it, and both guard against over-engineering.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid)** – the simplest solution that correctly solves the problem is usually the best; simple code is easier to read, test, debug, and change.
- **YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It)** – do not build functionality or abstractions on speculation about future needs; build only what the current requirement demands.
- **Balance with DRY** – DRY can tempt premature abstraction; KISS and YAGNI push back.
- **Rule of three** – wait for three genuine repetitions that change together before unifying.
- **Guiding phrase** – "duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction."
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh needs a simple way to transfer money between two accounts at National Bank of India. KISS says: write a straightforward transfer method that debits one and credits the other – do not build a configurable, plugin-based, rule-engine-driven transfer framework. YAGNI says: do not add support for fifteen currencies, scheduled transfers, and a message broker today just because someone imagines the bank might need them next year. If you build the imaginary mansion before anyone needs the extra rooms, you waste effort and create corridors nobody walks down.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Principle Balance
  ─────────────────

  KISS ──── "Simplest thing that works"
    │
    ├── YAGNI ── "Don't build until needed"
    │     │
    │     └── Resists: speculative patterns,
    │                  plugin frameworks,
    │                  message brokers
    │
    └── DRY ── "One home for each piece of knowledge"
          │
          └── Caution: can conflict with KISS/YAGNI
                       if applied to coincidental similarity

  Decision Flow:
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ Is this the same         │
  │ knowledge repeated?      │
  └────────┬─────────────────┘
      Yes  │          No
      ▼    │          ▼
  Extract  │   Keep separate
  (DRY)    │   (KISS + YAGNI)
           │
  ┌────────┴─────────────────┐
  │ Has it repeated 3 times? │
  └────────┬─────────────────┘
      Yes  │          No
      ▼    │          ▼
  Unify    │   Tolerate duplication
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
KISS and YAGNI are two principles that both push back against over-engineering. KISS says the simplest solution that correctly solves the problem is usually the best, because simple code is easier to read, test, debug, and change. YAGNI says do not build features or abstractions on speculation about future needs, because the imagined future rarely arrives as imagined, and meanwhile you pay for the guess in immediate complexity.

At National Bank of India, a colleague wanted to build a configurable rules engine with pluggable fee strategies and a Kafka topic to publish fee events, even though there was exactly one fee rule at the time. Rajesh wrote a plain fee method with a couple of constants. Later, when a genuine second rule actually arrived, extending the simple design was a tiny, obvious change.

The balancing act against DRY is critical. DRY is right that each piece of knowledge should have one home, but applied too eagerly it tempts premature abstraction. The classic trap is seeing two blocks that merely look alike and extracting them into one shared abstraction. If those blocks represent different rules that only coincide for now, the shared code becomes a mess of flags the moment they diverge. Rajesh lets KISS and YAGNI be the default and applies DRY only when the same knowledge genuinely repeats, often waiting for the rule of three.

Real YAGNI violations Rajesh has seen include building a plugin architecture for a service with only one implementation, adding a message broker when REST handles the load, and adding caching before measuring any performance problem. Each trades certain, immediate complexity for a speculative benefit that usually never materialises.

Remember one sentence: start with the simplest correct solution, do not build for imagined futures, and unify only when the same knowledge genuinely repeats and changes together.
